blogs.shortDescription: Door-to-door shipping to Kenya covers collection at the supplier, air or sea freight, KRA clearance, and delivery to your warehouse.
blogs.content:
Door-to-Door Shipping to Kenya

Door-to-door shipping to Kenya means one forwarder collects the cargo at the supplier, carries it by air or sea, clears it with KRA, and delivers it to your warehouse in Nairobi, Mombasa, or another town. You work with one team instead of a chain of separate agents. The part importers most often underestimate is the last mile after customs release.

What door-to-door shipping to Kenya includes

A complete move has three parts: origin handling, the flight or voyage, and delivery inside Kenya.

The three legs of the move

  • Collection from the supplier and export handling at origin
  • Air freight into JKIA or sea freight into Mombasa
  • Customs clearance, then delivery to your door

Transit time to plan for

Air freight often arrives within a few days. Sea freight usually takes several weeks, and clearance plus delivery add more time. Put that into the stock plan before the cargo leaves the supplier.

Ask for the full landed picture before you book: freight, duty, VAT, and delivery. A low ocean rate is not a cheap shipment if the truck to your warehouse was never included.

How to brief your forwarder

Send one clear note. The block below shows the shape of a booking brief. It is an example, not a live shipment.

Consignee: Your Company Ltd, Nairobi
Cargo: 12 cartons, 186 kg
Mode: Air freight to JKIA
Delivery: Warehouse, along Mombasa Road
Reference: GF20261001

Once the cargo is moving, track your Globeflight shipment with the consignment number you were given.

Why importers keep the job with one partner

Splitting the work between an origin agent, a carrier, a clearing agent, and a separate trucker leaves gaps. Door-to-door shipping to Kenya keeps collection, clearance, and delivery on one file, so a delay at the airport is handled by the same people who will bring the goods to your door.

blogs.title: Customs Clearance in Kenya: A Complete Guide for Importers | Globeflight
blogs.shortDescription: Navigating customs clearance in Kenya? Discover essential documents, KRA processes, import duties, and how Globeflight Kenya ensures fast, compliant cargo clearance.
blogs.content:
Importing goods into Kenya presents a massive opportunity for businesses. Whether you are bringing in electronics from China, auto parts from Japan, or textiles from India, the Kenyan market is vibrant and hungry for international products. However, the bridge between your global supplier and your local warehouse is paved with regulatory requirements.

Understanding customs clearance in Kenya is crucial. A single paperwork error can result in costly demurrage charges, cargo seizures, or delayed shipments. At Globeflight Kenya, we specialize in turning the complex web of import regulations into a seamless experience.

In this guide, we break down everything importers need to know about clearing goods through Kenyan borders.

Understanding the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) and the Simba System

The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) is the government body mandated to collect revenue, including customs duties. All customs clearance processes in Kenya are overseen by the KRA.

To modernize and streamline the process, KRA uses the Simba System (Customs Management System). This electronic portal allows clearing agents to lodge entries, pay taxes, and track the status of imported goods. As an importer, you must ensure your appointed clearing agent is well-versed in navigating the Simba system to avoid system-generated delays.

Essential import documents required in Kenya

Before your cargo even arrives at the Port of Mombasa or Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), you must have your documentation in order. Missing documents are the leading cause of clearance delays.

Here is the mandatory documentation checklist:

  • Commercial invoice: details the value of goods, currency, and terms of sale (Incoterms).
  • Bill of lading (B/L) or airway bill (AWB): the transport document issued by the carrier, acting as a receipt for the goods.
  • Packing list: details the weight, dimensions, and packaging of the cargo.
  • Certificate of origin: proves where the goods were manufactured. This is especially important if you are claiming preferential tariff rates under trade agreements like the East African Community (EAC) or AGOA.
  • Import Declaration Form (IDF): processed by your clearing agent before the goods arrive, allowing KRA to pre-alert the incoming cargo.
  • Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) certificate: also known as a KEBS certificate. For a specific list of regulated goods, the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) requires this certificate to prove the goods meet Kenyan quality standards before they leave the exporting country.

The step-by-step customs clearance process in Kenya

Navigating the clearance process requires strict adherence to KRA timelines. Here is the standard workflow managed by your clearing agent at Globeflight Kenya:

  1. Pre-arrival processing. Before the ship docks or the plane lands, your clearing agent lodges the IDF and prepares the customs entry using the commercial invoice and packing list.
  2. Payment of import duties and taxes. Using the Simba system, KRA calculates the taxes payable based on the HS Code (Harmonized System Code) of your goods. The importer or their agent must pay these taxes via a bank guarantor before clearance is approved.
  3. Cargo verification and inspection. Depending on the risk profile of your shipment, KRA may flag it for physical inspection or X-ray scanning. High-risk goods, or those with undervaluation suspicions, are subject to 100% physical verification.
  4. Cargo release and delivery. Once taxes are paid and inspections (if any) are cleared, KRA releases the goods. Your appointed transporter can then move the cargo to your designated destination, or it can be railed to the Inland Container Depots (ICDs) in Nairobi or Malaba.

Understanding import duties and taxes in Kenya

One of the most critical questions importers ask is, “How much will I pay in taxes?” The cost depends heavily on the HS Code of the product. The standard taxes applied include:

TaxWhat to expect
Customs dutyGenerally 0% to 35%, depending on the product. Goods originating from EAC partner states (Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi) often attract 0% duty.
Value Added Tax (VAT)Currently 16% on the customs value plus customs duty and other applicable taxes.
Excise dutyApplied to specific categories such as alcoholic beverages, tobacco, and certain motor vehicles.
Import Declaration Fee (IDF)Currently 2.5% of the customs value for commercial goods, with a minimum of KES 5,000.
Railway Development Levy (RDL)2% of the customs value, used to fund railway infrastructure.

Always consult your clearing agent to calculate the exact landed cost of your goods before shipping, so you are not surprised by the final bill.

Common customs clearance challenges, and how Globeflight Kenya handles them

Importing is not without hurdles. Here are common bottlenecks, and how an experienced logistics partner saves time and money.

Demurrage and port rent

If goods stay at the port past their free storage period, port authorities and shipping lines charge hefty daily fees.

The Globeflight approach: we pre-clear goods before the vessel arrives, so containers can leave the port within the free storage days.

Wrong HS Code classification

Using the wrong code leads to underpayment of taxes, which can bring heavy penalties and cargo confiscation.

The Globeflight approach: our licensed customs agents interpret the tariff carefully so the classification matches the goods.

Missing PVoC or KEBS certificates

Regulated goods that leave the origin country without the required certificate can be delayed, re-exported, or destroyed on arrival.

The Globeflight approach: we tell clients which goods need a standardization mark before they leave the origin country.

Why choose Globeflight Kenya for customs clearance

Navigating customs clearance in Kenya requires knowledge of local laws, working relationships with port authorities, and a proactive approach to problems. At Globeflight Kenya, we offer:

  • End-to-end logistics. From air freight and sea freight forwarding to customs clearance and last-mile delivery, we handle the supply chain as one job.
  • Licensed experts. Our team includes KRA-licensed clearing agents who understand the Simba system.
  • Transparency and speed. We share updates on your cargo and make tax payments promptly to avoid port storage fees.
  • A fit for the cargo. Whether you are a first-time importer or a large manufacturer, we shape the clearance around the goods, from perishables and project cargo to general merchandise.

Ready to clear your cargo?

Do not let paperwork stall the shipment. With Globeflight Kenya, the customs clearance process becomes a clear, managed sequence instead of a pile of separate tasks.

blogs.title: Freight Forwarding in Kenya: Everything Your Business Needs to Know
blogs.shortDescription: Learn how freight forwarding in Kenya works, from customs clearance to air and sea cargo. Discover how Globeflight Kenya moves your goods faster.
blogs.content:
Kenya is the commercial gateway to East Africa. With the Port of Mombasa on the Indian Ocean, Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in Nairobi, and road and rail corridors reaching Uganda, Rwanda, South Sudan, the DRC and beyond, the country is the starting point for much of the region's trade.

But moving goods in and out of Kenya involves paperwork, regulations and many moving parts. That is where a freight forwarder in Kenya comes in. This guide explains what freight forwarding is, how it works, and how to choose the right partner for your business.

What is freight forwarding?

Freight forwarding is the coordination of cargo from origin to destination. A freight forwarder does not usually own the ships or planes. Instead, they act as your intermediary, arranging transport, documentation, customs clearance, insurance and delivery so you do not have to manage each step yourself.

For businesses in Nairobi and across Kenya, a good forwarder saves time, reduces risk and often lowers the total cost of the move.

Core freight forwarding services in Kenya

Air freight

Air cargo through JKIA is the best choice for time-sensitive, high-value or perishable goods such as electronics, pharmaceuticals, fresh flowers and fresh produce. It is faster than sea freight, though usually more expensive per kilogram.

Sea freight via Mombasa

For bulky or heavy shipments, sea freight through the Port of Mombasa is the most cost-effective option. Businesses can choose between Full Container Load (FCL) for large volumes and Less than Container Load (LCL) for smaller consignments that share container space.

Road freight across East Africa

Road transport connects Nairobi and Mombasa to neighbouring countries, supporting cross-border trade within the East African Community (EAC). It offers flexibility and door-to-door delivery for regional shipments.

Customs clearance

Customs clearance is often where shipments get delayed. Kenya's import and export process involves correct tariff classification, duty and tax calculation, and accurate documentation submitted through the Kenya Revenue Authority's systems. A licensed clearing agent makes sure the paperwork is right the first time.

Warehousing and distribution

Secure storage, inventory handling and last-mile delivery keep the supply chain moving once cargo has cleared customs.

How the import process works in Kenya

Every shipment is different, but most imports follow these steps:

  1. Booking. Your forwarder arranges transport with the shipping line or airline.
  2. Documentation. Commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, and any permits required for the goods.
  3. Customs declaration. The entry is lodged, and duties and taxes are assessed.
  4. Inspection and release. Cargo may be inspected before release.
  5. Delivery. Goods are transported to your warehouse, shop or customer.

Requirements vary by product category, so confirm the current rules with your forwarder or the relevant authority before the cargo ships.

Why businesses choose a local logistics partner

Global carriers can move the cargo, but a local expert understands port procedures, documentation, regional routes, and who to call when something needs solving quickly.

A strong logistics company in Nairobi offers:

  • Local knowledge of Kenyan customs rules and port operations
  • One point of contact instead of juggling several vendors
  • Clear quotes so the costs are visible before you book
  • Shipment visibility so you know where the cargo is
  • A fit for the size of the job, from a small business to a large importer

Why choose Globeflight Kenya?

At Globeflight Kenya, we help businesses move goods with a clear plan. Based in Nairobi, we pair industry experience with a customer-first approach.

What sets the work apart:

  • End-to-end service: air, sea and road freight, plus customs clearance, handled under one roof
  • Reliable communication: updates from booking to delivery
  • A plan that fits the cargo: one pallet or a more complex supply chain
  • Competitive pricing: a clear quote, without surprise lines at the end

Tips to ship smarter in Kenya

  • Plan early. Book cargo space ahead, especially in peak seasons.
  • Get the documents right. Errors in invoices and declarations are the most common cause of delay.
  • Know your Incoterms. Terms such as FOB, CIF and DAP decide who pays for what, and who carries the risk.
  • Insure the cargo. Goods in transit can be damaged or lost.
  • Choose the right mode. Match speed and cost to the nature of the goods.

Book the space and finish the documents before the cargo is ready to leave. Most delays in Kenya start with a missing line on an invoice, not with the ship or the aircraft.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to clear goods at Mombasa Port?

Clearance time depends on documentation, cargo type and inspection requirements. Accurate paperwork and an experienced clearing agent can significantly shorten the process.

What documents do I need to import goods into Kenya?

Typically a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, and any product-specific permits or certificates. Your forwarder can confirm exactly what your cargo needs.

What is the difference between FCL and LCL shipping?

FCL means you book an entire container. LCL means your cargo shares a container with other shippers, which suits smaller volumes.

Can Globeflight Kenya handle shipments to other East African countries?

Yes. We arrange regional road freight and the documents for cargo moving between Kenya and other East African Community countries.

How do I get a freight quote?

Send the cargo details, origin, destination and timeline, and the team will reply with a tailored quote. You can contact Globeflight Kenya or track a shipment that is already on the move.

Ready to move your cargo?

Whether you are importing machinery, exporting produce or shipping across East Africa, Globeflight Kenya can take the logistics off your desk.

blogs.title: KRA Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD): 10 Things Every Kenyan Importer Must Know Before Shipping
blogs.shortDescription: Learn what Kenyan importers need to know about KRA's Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD), including documents, ACD Reference Numbers, loading requirements and the 1 September 2026 deadline.
blogs.content:
Importing goods into Kenya is becoming increasingly digital, and businesses that ship goods internationally need to keep up with new customs requirements. One of the most important recent changes is the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) platform.

For importers, exporters, freight forwarders, shipping lines, customs agents and other stakeholders, understanding the ACD requirement is essential if you want to avoid shipping delays and compliance problems.

The KRA ACD platform officially launched on 3 August 2026 for containerised cargo destined for Kenyan ports. The system requires cargo information to be submitted before loading, so Customs receives advance information about the shipment.

With 1 September 2026 approaching, Kenyan importers need to know what the ACD means, who obtains it, which documents are required, and what to do before the next shipment leaves the country of origin.

Here are 10 things every Kenyan importer should know about the Advance Cargo Declaration.

1. What is the Advance Cargo Declaration?

The Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) is a digital pre-loading cargo declaration introduced by KRA for applicable containerised shipments destined for Kenyan ports.

It gives Customs advance information about the cargo, including the shipper or exporter, the vessel, the cargo, and the supporting shipping documents.

The purpose is to improve:

  • Customs compliance
  • Cargo visibility
  • Risk assessment
  • Supply-chain transparency
  • Monitoring of imports
  • Efficiency in customs processing

According to the official KRA ACD platform, every shipment unloaded at a Kenyan port must be covered by a validated declaration.

In simple terms, the ACD gives Customs information about your cargo before it reaches Kenya.

2. The ACD is already in effect

This matters for businesses planning shipments now.

The ACD platform officially launched on 3 August 2026 for containerised cargo destined for Kenyan ports. KRA's public notice states that exporters shipping goods to Kenya are required to obtain an ACD Reference Code at the point of loading.

Do not wait until the container is already on the water before asking whether an ACD is required. The process has to be considered before the cargo is loaded.

3. From 1 September 2026, carriers will check the ACD before loading

One of the most important dates is 1 September 2026.

According to a recent carrier advisory, from 1 September vessel carriers will be required to validate the ACD Reference Number before loading, and to load containers at origin only when a valid ACD Reference Number has been obtained.

Do not wait until the shipment is about to depart before confirming the ACD. If the reference is missing, the container may not be loaded and could be rolled to a later vessel.

For businesses with tight delivery schedules, that can affect inventory, production, customer orders and cash flow.

4. Who is responsible for obtaining the ACD?

The ACD process involves several parties. The official KRA platform states that the ACD must be obtained at the port of loading by the shipper, exporter, or freight forwarder.

Kenyan importers should speak with their overseas suppliers and logistics partners so the requirement is actually being handled.

If a Kenyan company buys machinery from China, the importer should confirm with the supplier or the appointed freight forwarder:

Who is handling the ACD application, and when will the ACD Reference Number be available?

That question prevents problems later.

5. What documents are required?

According to KRA's official ACD platform and public notice, the documents required include:

  • Draft bill of lading
  • Commercial invoice
  • Freight invoice
  • Export declaration

The documents should be clear and readable. ACD drafts should also contain the relevant container information and HS Codes. Ask suppliers for accurate documents early.

6. The ACD reference number must appear on the bill of lading

Obtaining an ACD is not the end of the process. The ACD Reference Number must be endorsed on the bill of lading.

KRA states that the reference code generated after approval must be endorsed on the bill of lading before the shipment proceeds to a Kenyan port. Check the shipping documents carefully.

Before the shipment departs, confirm each step:

  1. The ACD has been obtained.
  2. The reference number has been verified.
  3. The reference number appears on the bill of lading.

An error in the reference number, or a missing number, creates avoidable complications.

7. Accurate information matters

The ACD is only as good as the information supplied about the shipment. Keep these details consistent across the documents:

  • Shipper details
  • Consignee details
  • Cargo description
  • Container numbers
  • Quantity
  • Weight
  • Commercial value
  • HS Codes
  • Vessel information
  • Bill of lading details

If information changes after an ACD has been issued, the relevant parties should check whether the declaration or the shipping documents need to be amended. The information sent to Customs should match the cargo that is actually shipped.

8. What happens if you ship without a valid ACD?

KRA's official ACD platform warns that failure to obtain an ACD can result in fines, delays, rejection of cargo at the port of entry and, in severe cases, seizure or confiscation.

The carrier guidance also states that from 1 September 2026, containers without a valid ACD Reference Number may not be eligible for loading and could be rolled to a later vessel.

The ACD is not an optional form. For a business, skipping it can lead to:

  • Shipment delays
  • Additional costs
  • Missed delivery schedules
  • Inventory shortages
  • Unhappy customers
  • Further customs complications

9. The ACD changes how importers should plan

Many businesses think about customs clearance only when the cargo reaches Kenya. The ACD asks for a different habit: customs compliance starts before the cargo leaves the country of origin.

Involve your logistics and customs partners early. A useful pre-shipment checklist has three stages.

Before placing the order

  • Confirm the product requirements.
  • Confirm the supplier's export capability.
  • Check applicable permits and certifications.
  • Determine the correct HS Code.

Before the cargo is loaded

  • Confirm the shipping documents.
  • Confirm the ACD requirement.
  • Submit the required ACD documents.
  • Obtain the ACD Reference Number.
  • Make sure the reference is on the bill of lading.

Before the vessel departs

  • Confirm that the shipping line has the required ACD information.
  • Verify that the documentation is accurate.
  • Share the final documents with your clearing or logistics partner.

10. Work with a logistics partner who knows the process

International shipping is more than moving a box from one country to another. Suppliers, exporters, shipping lines, freight forwarders, customs agents, government agencies, documents and delivery all have to line up. The ACD makes that early coordination more important.

An experienced logistics partner can help coordinate:

  • International freight
  • Shipping documentation
  • ACD requirements
  • Customs clearance
  • Cargo tracking
  • Import compliance
  • Warehousing
  • Local transportation
  • Final delivery

At Globeflight Kenya, businesses need more than a truck or a booking. They need the same team to stay with the file from origin through delivery. Our work covers international freight, customs clearance, warehousing, distribution and the rest of the supply chain around the move. Talk to Globeflight Kenya before the next container is booked.

A simple ACD checklist for Kenyan importers

Before the next container is shipped to Kenya, work through this list:

  1. Confirm whether the shipment falls under the ACD requirement.
  2. Confirm who will apply for the ACD.
  3. Prepare the draft bill of lading.
  4. Prepare the commercial invoice.
  5. Prepare the freight invoice.
  6. Prepare the export declaration.
  7. Check that the cargo details and HS Codes are accurate.
  8. Obtain the ACD Reference Number before loading.
  9. Confirm that the reference number is endorsed on the bill of lading.
  10. Confirm with the carrier or freight forwarder that the shipment is compliant before loading.

A few minutes of preparation can prevent a much larger problem later.

Frequently asked questions

Is the ACD mandatory in Kenya?

The KRA ACD platform states that the ACD is mandatory for applicable containerised shipments destined for Kenya, and that shipments unloaded at Kenyan ports must be covered by a validated declaration.

When did the ACD platform become operational?

The official launch for containerised cargo destined for Kenyan ports was 3 August 2026.

What changes on 1 September 2026?

From 1 September 2026, carriers are expected to validate the ACD Reference Number before loading covered containers at origin.

Who applies for the ACD?

The shipper, exporter or freight forwarder can apply for the ACD at the port of loading.

What documents are required?

The official KRA guidance lists the draft bill of lading, commercial invoice, freight invoice and export declaration.

Where can I access the ACD platform?

The official platform is KRA's Advance Cargo Declaration platform.

Final thoughts

The Advance Cargo Declaration is an important change in Kenya's trade and customs environment. For Kenyan importers, the lesson is simple: do not wait until the cargo reaches Kenya to think about compliance.

The ACD process starts at the port of loading. Importers need to speak with overseas suppliers, freight forwarders and shipping lines well before the cargo is loaded. With the 1 September 2026 carrier check approaching, review current import procedures and make sure suppliers and logistics partners understand the requirement.

Accurate documents, early preparation and clear communication reduce avoidable disruption. Globeflight Kenya helps businesses with international freight, customs clearance, warehousing and the requirements that come with them.

Planning the next shipment to Kenya? Talk to Globeflight Kenya and let the team walk through the logistics with you. You can also track a shipment that is already moving.

blogs.title: How to Import Goods into Kenya: A Step-by-Step Guide for Businesses
blogs.shortDescription: Learn how to import goods into Kenya step by step. Discover import documents, customs clearance, duties, permits, ACD requirements, freight and delivery.
blogs.content:
Importing goods into Kenya can be an excellent opportunity for businesses looking to source products, raw materials, machinery, equipment, or finished goods from international markets. However, the importation process involves more than simply purchasing goods from an overseas supplier and arranging transportation.

Importers need to consider documentation, customs requirements, taxes and duties, product standards, permits, shipping arrangements, customs clearance, and final delivery.

For businesses that are new to international trade, these requirements can seem complicated. Understanding the import process from the beginning can help you avoid unnecessary delays, unexpected costs, and compliance problems.

In this guide, we explain how to import goods into Kenya step by step, from finding a supplier to getting your goods cleared and delivered.

What Does Importing Goods into Kenya Involve?

Importing means bringing goods into Kenya from another country for commercial or other permitted purposes.

The process normally involves several parties, including:

·        The importer

·        Overseas supplier or exporter

·        Freight forwarder

·        Shipping line or airline

·        Customs clearing agent

·        Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA)

·        Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS), where applicable

·        Other government agencies depending on the type of goods

For commercial imports, KRA advises importers to engage a licensed customs clearing agent to process customs documentation and clearance.

The exact requirements can vary depending on the type of goods, country of origin, mode of transport, and applicable regulations.

Step 1: Identify the Goods You Want to Import

The first step is to clearly identify the products you intend to import.

Before placing an order, determine:

·        What the product is

·        Quantity required

·        Country of origin

·        Product specifications

·        Intended use

·        Approximate value

·        Weight and dimensions

·        Whether the product is restricted or regulated

This information is important because different products can have different customs classifications, tax treatment, standards requirements, and import permits.

For example, importing electronics may involve different regulatory requirements from importing industrial machinery, food products, pharmaceuticals, or automotive parts.

Understanding your product before purchasing it can prevent problems later in the import process.

Step 2: Find and Verify Your Overseas Supplier

Once you know what you want to import, the next step is finding a reliable supplier.

Businesses can source products from countries such as China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, and many other international markets.

However, price should not be the only consideration when selecting a supplier.

Before making payment, consider:

·        Supplier reputation

·        Product quality

·        Previous customer reviews

·        Production capacity

·        Payment terms

·        Lead times

·        Export experience

·        Shipping arrangements

·        Ability to provide accurate commercial documentation

A supplier that provides incomplete or inaccurate documents can create problems during customs clearance.

Step 3: Understand the Cost of Importing

One of the biggest mistakes new importers make is looking only at the supplier’s product price.

The actual cost of importing goods can include several components.

These may include:

Product cost + international freight + insurance where applicable + duties and taxes + customs-related charges + port/airport charges + clearing fees + local transportation + warehousing where applicable

The applicable taxes and duties depend on the product classification, customs value, and relevant Kenyan laws and regulations. KRA notes that duty rates vary according to the goods and the applicable tariff.

Before placing a large order, ask your logistics or customs partner to help you understand the potential landed cost.

This allows you to determine whether importing the product is commercially viable before committing your capital.

Step 4: Determine the Correct HS Code

Every internationally traded product needs to be classified using a Harmonized System (HS) Code.

HS Codes are used by customs authorities to identify products and determine applicable duties, taxes, restrictions, and regulatory requirements.

Correct classification is extremely important.

An incorrect HS Code can result in:

·        Incorrect duty assessment

·        Customs queries

·        Delays

·        Additional costs

·        Compliance issues

Do not simply rely on the supplier’s classification without verification. The appropriate classification should be confirmed based on the actual product and applicable customs requirements.

Step 5: Check Whether Your Goods Require Permits or Certification

Not every product can be imported into Kenya under the same conditions.

Some goods are subject to specific regulatory requirements, permits, licences, inspections, or standards.

Depending on the product, requirements may involve agencies such as:

·        Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS)

·        Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS)

·        Pharmacy and Poisons Board

·        Communications Authority of Kenya

·        Department of Veterinary Services

·        Other relevant government agencies

For regulated products, KRA’s import guidance specifically identifies requirements such as a Certificate of Conformity (CoC) from a PVoC agent and an Import Standardization Mark (ISM) where applicable.

It is therefore important to check the requirements before the goods are shipped, rather than discovering a missing permit after the cargo arrives in Kenya.

The Kenya Trade Portal is an important resource for checking government requirements relating to imports and exports.

Step 6: Prepare the Required Import Documents

Documentation is one of the most important parts of international shipping.

Depending on the shipment, common import documents may include:

·        Commercial Invoice

·        Packing List

·        Bill of Lading for sea freight

·        Air Waybill for air freight

·        Certificate of Origin

·        Import Declaration Form (IDF)

·        Import permits or licences where applicable

·        Certificate of Conformity where applicable

·        Freight invoice

·        Purchase order or contract

·        Taxpayer/PIN documentation

·        Other documents required for specific products

KRA’s current import guidance lists several of these documents and states that the customs clearing agent uses the information to make the customs declaration.

The documents should be accurate and consistent.

For example, the product description, quantity, value, weights, and other shipment details should correspond across the relevant documents.

Step 7: Choose Between Air Freight and Sea Freight

The next decision is choosing the right mode of transportation.

Air Freight

Air freight is generally suitable when:

·        Goods are time-sensitive

·        The shipment is relatively small

·        Faster delivery is important

·        The goods have a high value relative to their weight

Sea Freight

Sea freight is often suitable when:

·        Shipping larger volumes

·        Importing heavy or bulky goods

·        Cost efficiency is a priority

·        Delivery time is less urgent

Choosing between air and sea freight depends on your product, budget, urgency, shipment size, and supply chain requirements.

A good freight forwarding partner can help you evaluate the options before booking the shipment.

Step 8: Prepare for the Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD)

Kenya’s import environment is becoming increasingly digital.

The Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) is now an important requirement for cargo destined for Kenyan ports. The official KRA ACD platform states that every shipment unloaded at a Kenyan port must be covered by a validated declaration.

For containerised cargo, KRA’s ACD platform states that the shipper or exporter must obtain the ACD Reference Code at the port of loading before the cargo is loaded.

The reference code must also be correctly included on the Bill of Lading.

The ACD process requires documents such as:

·        Bill of Lading

·        Commercial Invoice

·        Freight Invoice

·        Export Declaration

The ACD platform also states that the declaration should be validated at least five days before vessel arrival.

Because the ACD process involves the shipper, exporter, freight forwarder, and shipping line, early communication is essential.

Step 9: Arrange International Shipping

Once the documentation and regulatory requirements are in order, the shipment can be arranged.

Your freight forwarder can coordinate important aspects of the shipment, including:

·        Cargo collection

·        Export documentation

·        Freight booking

·        Shipping arrangements

·        Cargo tracking

·        Communication with the supplier

·        Coordination with the shipping line or airline

At this stage, accurate information is critical.

Changes to the product description, quantity, value, or shipping documents after booking can create additional complications.

Step 10: Customs Declaration and Clearance

When the goods arrive in Kenya, customs clearance becomes a major part of the import process.

The appointed customs clearing agent prepares and submits the customs declaration using the relevant customs systems and supporting documentation.

KRA states that the customs agent processes import documentation electronically and assists with clearing goods on behalf of the importer.

Customs may assess:

·        Import duty

·        VAT

·        Excise duty where applicable

·        Import-related fees and levies

·        Other applicable charges

The actual amount depends on the goods, customs value, classification, and applicable legislation.

Importers should therefore avoid assuming that every product attracts the same rate.

Step 11: Customs Verification and Release

Depending on the customs process and risk assessment, a shipment may undergo document review, verification, inspection, or other enforcement measures.

KRA’s published clearance guidance describes a process involving customs declaration, payment of applicable taxes, processing, verification where required, and eventual clearance and release for compliant declarations.

Once the required procedures have been completed and applicable payments made, the goods can be released from customs.

This is where having accurate documentation and an experienced customs clearance partner can make a significant difference.

Step 12: Transport Your Goods to Their Final Destination

Customs clearance is not necessarily the end of the logistics process.

After release, the goods may need to be transported to:

·        Your warehouse

·        Retail location

·        Factory

·        Office

·        Distribution centre

·        Customer

Businesses importing regularly may also benefit from professional warehousing and distribution services.

Instead of managing separate providers for freight, customs, storage, and delivery, an integrated logistics partner can coordinate several stages of the supply chain.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Importing into Kenya

Importing can become expensive when businesses make avoidable mistakes.

Here are some common problems to watch out for:

1. Choosing a Supplier Based Only on Price

The cheapest supplier may not provide the best quality, documentation, or shipping support.

2. Incorrect Product Classification

Using an incorrect HS Code can affect customs assessment and compliance.

3. Missing Import Permits

Some products require regulatory approval before importation.

4. Inaccurate Documentation

Differences between invoices, packing lists, Bills of Lading, and customs declarations can result in queries or delays.

5. Underestimating the Total Import Cost

The purchase price is only one part of the total landed cost.

6. Waiting Until Cargo Arrives to Plan Clearance

Customs preparation should begin before the shipment reaches Kenya.

7. Ignoring New Regulatory Requirements

Import regulations and digital customs procedures can change. The ACD is a good example of why importers should keep up with current requirements.

How a Freight Forwarding Partner Can Help

International importing involves multiple stages and stakeholders.

A professional freight forwarding and logistics partner can help coordinate:

·        International transportation

·        Shipping documentation

·        Customs clearance

·        Regulatory requirements

·        Cargo tracking

·        Warehousing

·        Local transportation

·        Final delivery

This can reduce the administrative burden on businesses and allow them to focus on their core operations.

Frequently Asked Questions About Importing Goods into Kenya

What documents do I need to import goods into Kenya?

Common documents include a commercial invoice, packing list, Bill of Lading or Air Waybill, certificate of origin, applicable permits, and other customs and regulatory documents. Requirements vary depending on the type of goods.

Do I need a customs clearing agent?

For commercial imports, KRA states that importers should engage a licensed customs clearing agent to process the customs documentation and clear the goods.

How much tax will I pay when importing goods into Kenya?

There is no single rate that applies to all imported goods. The amount depends on the product classification, customs value, applicable duty rate, VAT, excise duty where applicable, and other relevant fees or levies.

What is an HS Code?

An HS Code is a standardized classification used to identify goods in international trade. It helps customs authorities determine applicable duties, taxes, and regulatory requirements.

Do all imported goods require permits?

No. Requirements depend on the type of goods. Certain regulated or restricted products may require permits, licences, inspection, or certification.

What is the ACD in Kenya?

The Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) is a cargo declaration submitted before arrival for cargo destined for Kenyan ports. KRA’s official ACD platform states that every shipment unloaded at a Kenyan port must have a validated declaration.

Final Thoughts

Importing goods into Kenya does not have to be complicated when the process is properly planned.

The key is to start preparing before the goods leave the supplier’s country. Confirm the product requirements, choose a reliable supplier, understand your landed costs, prepare accurate documentation, arrange the appropriate freight service, meet applicable regulatory requirements, and work with an experienced customs clearance partner.

Most importantly, do not treat customs clearance as something that happens only after your shipment arrives. Successful importing requires coordination from the moment you place your order until the goods reach their final destination.

blogs.title: KRA Introduces Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD): What Importers and Exporters Need to Know

blogs.content:
International trade is becoming increasingly digital, and customs authorities around the world are adopting technology to improve cargo visibility, strengthen compliance, and facilitate legitimate trade. In Kenya, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), through its Customs and Border Control function, has introduced the Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) Platform for cargo destined for Kenyan ports.

The new system is an important development for importers, exporters, freight forwarders, shipping lines, carriers, and clearing agents involved in international trade with Kenya.

With the implementation of the ACD platform, businesses involved in shipping cargo to Kenya will need to understand the new requirements, the application process, and how the declaration may affect their import and logistics operations.

What Is the Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD)?

The Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) is a mandatory cargo declaration that provides customs authorities with detailed information about a shipment before the cargo arrives at a Kenyan port.

The declaration contains information relating to the cargo, vessel, exporter, and other relevant shipment details. The official ACD platform also notes that the system may be known in other jurisdictions by names such as CTN, ECTN, BSC, or BESC.

The purpose of the ACD is to allow Customs to receive and assess cargo information in advance, helping improve regulatory compliance, cargo monitoring, and supply-chain transparency.

According to the official ACD platform, every shipment unloaded at a Kenyan port must be covered by a validated Advance Cargo Declaration.

When Will the ACD Platform Go Live?

The Kenya Revenue Authority’s Advance Cargo Declaration Platform is scheduled to officially go live on Monday, 3 August 2026, for containerised cargo destined for Kenyan ports.

From the implementation date, the shipper or exporter must apply for and obtain an ACD Reference Code at the port of loading before the cargo is loaded.

The ACD Reference Code must then be correctly included on the Bill of Lading. Shipping lines, carriers, shipowners, and their appointed agents are expected to request the reference code before issuing the final Bill of Lading.

Importers and exporters should therefore begin preparing early to avoid customs and shipping delays.

Who Is Affected by the Advance Cargo Declaration?

The ACD requirement affects several stakeholders involved in the international movement of cargo, including:

Importers

Businesses importing goods into Kenya should ensure that their overseas suppliers, exporters, and logistics partners understand the ACD requirements before the shipment is loaded.

Exporters and Shippers

The shipper or exporter is required to apply for the Advance Cargo Declaration at the port of loading.

Freight Forwarders

Freight forwarders may assist shippers and exporters with preparing and submitting the required information and supporting documents.

Shipping Lines and Carriers

Shipping lines, shipowners, carriers, and appointed agents are expected to request the ACD Reference Code and ensure it is correctly reflected on the Bill of Lading.

Clearing Agents

Clearing agents may require the ACD details when supporting the customs clearance process after the cargo arrives in Kenya.

Because multiple parties are involved, communication between the importer, exporter, freight forwarder, shipping line, and clearing agent is essential.

What Documents Are Required for an ACD Application?

According to the official ACD platform, applicants should prepare clear and readable documentation before submitting their declaration.

The required documents include:

·       Draft Bill of Lading

·       Commercial Invoice

·       Freight Invoice

·       Export Declaration

ACD drafts should also include important shipment details such as container information and the relevant Harmonized System (HS) Codes.

Providing accurate and consistent information is extremely important. Differences between the ACD application, commercial invoice, Bill of Lading, and other shipping documents may lead to additional queries or delays.

How Does the Advance Cargo Declaration Process Work?

The ACD process is designed to be completed electronically through the official platform.

The general process involves:

Step 1: Register and Prepare Your Documents

The shipper, exporter, or authorised freight forwarder prepares the required shipping documents and registers on the official ACD platform.

Step 2: Submit the Cargo Declaration

The applicant submits the cargo information and supporting documents through the online platform.

Step 3: Obtain the ACD Reference Code

Once the declaration is approved, an ACD Reference Code is issued.

Step 4: Include the Reference Code on the Bill of Lading

The ACD Reference Code must be correctly endorsed on the Bill of Lading.

Step 5: Validate the Declaration Before Vessel Arrival

The official ACD platform indicates that the declaration should be validated at least five days before the vessel arrives.

Step 6: Proceed with Customs Clearance

Once the cargo arrives in Kenya, the relevant customs and clearance procedures can proceed with the shipment supported by the required ACD information.

Why Is the ACD Important for Importers?

The introduction of the Advance Cargo Declaration represents a significant change in the way cargo information is submitted and processed before arrival.

For importers, one of the biggest benefits is improved visibility over the shipment process.

The ACD system is designed to help authorities:

·       Receive cargo information before arrival

·       Improve cargo monitoring

·       Strengthen customs compliance

·       Improve supply-chain transparency

·       Identify potential risks earlier

·       Support more efficient customs processing

For businesses, better preparation and accurate information can help reduce avoidable delays caused by missing or inconsistent shipping documentation.

The official platform states that a valid declaration supports customs processing and helps improve cargo tracking and supply-chain transparency.

What Happens If a Shipment Does Not Have a Valid ACD?

Failure to obtain the required Advance Cargo Declaration can create serious compliance and operational challenges.

The official ACD platform warns that failure to obtain an ACD may result in fines, delays, or rejection of cargo at the port of entry. In severe cases, non-compliance may also result in seizure or confiscation.

For this reason, importers should not wait until the cargo is already in transit before confirming whether the ACD requirement has been met.

The best approach is to confirm the requirement early with the exporter, shipping line, freight forwarder, or customs clearance partner.

How Can Importers Prepare for the ACD Requirement?

Businesses importing goods into Kenya can take several practical steps to prepare.

1. Speak to Your Overseas Supplier Early

Make sure your supplier or exporter understands that cargo destined for Kenya may require an Advance Cargo Declaration before loading.

2. Prepare Accurate Documentation

Ensure that the commercial invoice, freight invoice, draft Bill of Lading, export declaration, container details, and HS Codes are accurate and consistent.

3. Confirm Who Will Apply for the ACD

The importer should establish whether the shipper, exporter, freight forwarder, or another authorised party will handle the application.

4. Verify the ACD Reference Code

Before the shipment is loaded, confirm that the required ACD Reference Code has been obtained.

5. Ensure the Code Appears on the Bill of Lading

The ACD Reference Code must be correctly reflected on the Bill of Lading.

6. Work With an Experienced Logistics Partner

International shipping involves multiple documents, stakeholders, and regulatory requirements. Working with an experienced freight forwarding and customs clearance partner can help reduce the risk of avoidable errors.

What Does the ACD Mean for Freight Forwarding and Customs Clearance?

The introduction of the ACD highlights the importance of early preparation in international logistics.

Customs clearance should not begin only when cargo arrives at the port. Many of the most important compliance steps take place before the shipment is loaded and transported.

This means importers need better coordination between:

·       Overseas suppliers

·       Exporters

·       Freight forwarders

·       Shipping lines

·       Customs agents

·       Government agencies

An experienced logistics partner can help coordinate the documentation and information required throughout the shipping process.

For businesses importing goods into Kenya, professional freight forwarding and customs brokerage support can make it easier to manage evolving regulatory requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions About the ACD

Is the Advance Cargo Declaration mandatory?

Yes. The official ACD platform states that cargo unloaded at Kenyan ports must be covered by a validated Advance Cargo Declaration.

Who applies for the ACD?

The shipper, exporter, or freight forwarder may apply for the ACD at the port of loading.

When should the ACD be obtained?

The ACD Reference Code should be obtained before the cargo is loaded, and the official platform indicates that validation should take place at least five days before vessel arrival.

What documents are needed?

The key documents include the Draft Bill of Lading, Commercial Invoice, Freight Invoice, and Export Declaration. The ACD draft should also include container details and HS Codes.

Where can I access the official ACD platform?

Importers, exporters, freight forwarders, and other stakeholders should use the official Kenya Revenue Authority Customs and Border Control ACD platform for applications and guidance: Official KRA ACD Platform

Conclusion

The introduction of the Advance Cargo Declaration (ACD) Platform is an important development in Kenya’s customs and international trade environment.

By requiring cargo information to be submitted and validated before arrival, the system is designed to improve cargo visibility, strengthen compliance, and promote greater transparency throughout the supply chain.

For importers and exporters, the key takeaway is simple: prepare early, provide accurate information, and ensure the ACD requirement is handled before cargo is loaded.

As customs procedures continue to become more digital, businesses that maintain accurate documentation and work with experienced logistics partners will be better positioned to avoid unnecessary delays and compliance challenges.

Introduction

International shipping powers global trade, but customs delays remain one of the biggest challenges for businesses and individuals alike. A shipment can arrive at the destination port or airport on schedule, only to get held up for days or weeks during clearance.

At Globeflight Kenya, we’ve helped thousands of clients navigate these hurdles successfully. In 2026, with evolving trade regulations, stricter compliance checks, and ongoing supply chain pressures, understanding why delays occur is essential. This guide shares the most common causes of customs delays and practical tips to avoid them—so your goods keep moving.

Why Do Customs Delays Happen? The Top Causes

Most customs delays stem from preventable issues rather than random chance. Here are the leading culprits:

  1. Incomplete or Inaccurate Documentation This is by far the #1 reason shipments get held. Missing commercial invoices, packing lists, bills of lading, or certificates of origin can stop clearance immediately. Even small errors—like typos in addresses, mismatched quantities, or vague product descriptions—trigger flags.

  2. Incorrect HS Codes or Product Classification Every item needs the right Harmonized System (HS) code. Misclassification leads to wrong duty calculations, additional scrutiny, or outright rejection. Customs authorities use these codes to determine tariffs, restrictions, and inspection needs.

  3. Valuation Issues and Under-Declaration Declaring goods at the wrong value (too low or inconsistent with invoices) raises red flags. Customs may question the transaction value, especially if freight, insurance, or other costs are mishandled.

  4. Missing Licenses, Permits, or Regulatory Approvals Restricted or regulated goods—such as electronics, batteries, pharmaceuticals, food, or chemicals—often require extra certifications. Without them, shipments face holds or seizures.

  5. Random or Targeted Inspections Even compliant shipments can be selected for physical inspection. High-risk categories (e.g., lithium batteries or sensitive tech) increase the odds. Discrepancies found during inspection extend delays.

  6. Unpaid Duties, Taxes, or Fees Customs won't release goods until all applicable duties, VAT, or taxes are settled.

  7. External Factors Port congestion, labor shortages, seasonal peaks, weather, or changing trade regulations can compound paperwork issues.

How to Avoid Customs Delays: Proven Strategies from Globeflight Kenya

Drawing from our daily experience handling shipments across Africa and worldwide, here’s how to minimize risks:

·       Prepare Documentation in Advance — Double-check all paperwork 48–72 hours before shipment. Use clear, detailed product descriptions that match exactly what's inside the package. Include accurate values, quantities, weights, and Incoterms.

  • Stay Ahead of Country-Specific Rules — Regulations differ by destination. We keep our clients updated on the latest requirements for major markets.

  • File in Advance and Track Proactively — Use pre-arrival filing options and monitor your shipment closely.

  • Declare Values Accurately and Pay Fees Promptly — Avoid undervaluation, which often leads to penalties and longer holds.

  • Leverage Professional Support — For frequent or complex shipments, trust specialists who understand both Kenyan export rules and international import requirements.

What to Do If Your Shipment Is Stuck in Customs

Contact your logistics partner immediately. At Globeflight Kenya, our team works quickly to resolve holds by providing required information and coordinating with authorities.

Conclusion

Customs delays don’t have to be part of your shipping experience. With proper preparation, accurate documentation, and the right partner, you can achieve faster clearance and more predictable delivery times.

Can a freight forwarder really help avoid customs delays? Yes. Experienced partners like Globeflight Kenya manage compliance and documentation proactively.

What documents are most commonly missing? Commercial invoices, accurate packing lists, and required permits or certificates.

blogs.content:
In today's competitive business environment, efficient warehousing plays a critical role in supply chain success. Whether you're an e-commerce retailer, importer, manufacturer, or distributor, choosing the right warehousing partner can significantly impact your operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and profitability.

A warehouse is more than just a storage facility. It serves as a strategic hub where inventory is received, managed, stored, picked, packed, and dispatched to customers. The right warehousing partner helps streamline operations, reduce costs, improve order accuracy, and support business growth.

However, with numerous warehousing providers available, selecting the best fit for your business can be challenging. This guide outlines seven essential factors to consider when choosing a warehousing partner and how the right provider can strengthen your supply chain.

1. Evaluate Location and Accessibility

Location is one of the most important factors when selecting a warehousing partner. A strategically located warehouse can reduce transportation costs, improve delivery times, and enhance overall supply chain efficiency.

When evaluating warehouse locations, consider:

  • Proximity to your customers

  • Access to major highways, airports, and ports

  • Availability of transportation networks

  • Regional and international distribution requirements

For businesses operating in East Africa, choosing a warehouse with convenient access to major transport routes can significantly improve delivery performance and reduce logistics costs.

A strategically located warehouse also allows businesses to respond more quickly to changing customer demands and market opportunities.

2. Assess Storage Capacity and Scalability

Business needs evolve over time. Seasonal fluctuations, new product lines, and market expansion can all affect storage requirements.

Your warehousing partner should be able to accommodate both your current inventory needs and future growth plans.

Look for providers that offer:

  • Flexible storage solutions

  • Short-term and long-term storage options

  • Scalable warehouse space

  • Capacity to handle peak seasons

A scalable warehousing solution ensures that your business can grow without experiencing disruptions or costly relocations.

3. Review Warehouse Technology and Inventory Management Systems

Modern warehousing relies heavily on technology. Advanced warehouse management systems (WMS) improve inventory visibility, accuracy, and operational efficiency.

Before selecting a warehouse provider, evaluate their technology capabilities, including:

  • Real-time inventory tracking

  • Barcode scanning systems

  • Automated stock management

  • Inventory reporting and analytics

  • Order tracking and fulfillment monitoring

Technology-driven warehousing reduces human error and enables businesses to make informed decisions based on accurate inventory data.

Businesses that invest in advanced inventory management often experience improved order accuracy, faster fulfillment times, and reduced operational costs.

4. Examine Security and Safety Standards

Inventory represents a significant business investment. Protecting that inventory should be a top priority.

A reliable warehousing partner should maintain robust security and safety measures, including:

  • 24/7 surveillance systems

  • Controlled facility access

  • Fire prevention and suppression systems

  • Alarm monitoring

  • Secure inventory handling procedures

Additionally, warehouse operators should comply with industry safety standards and implement procedures that minimize risks to both inventory and personnel.

Strong security measures help prevent theft, damage, and disruptions that can negatively impact business operations.

5. Consider Industry Experience and Expertise

Not all warehouses are equipped to handle every type of product.

Certain industries require specialized storage conditions, handling procedures, and regulatory compliance. Examples include:

  • Pharmaceuticals

  • Electronics

  • Automotive parts

  • Consumer goods

  • Industrial equipment

An experienced warehousing partner understands industry-specific requirements and can help businesses avoid costly mistakes.

When evaluating providers, ask about:

  • Industry experience

  • Client references

  • Regulatory compliance knowledge

  • Specialized handling capabilities

A provider with proven expertise is more likely to deliver reliable and efficient warehousing services.

6. Evaluate Value-Added Services

Many businesses benefit from warehousing partners that offer services beyond storage.

Value-added services can help streamline operations and reduce the need for multiple service providers.

Common value-added services include:

  • Pick and pack services

  • Inventory management

  • Distribution and transportation

  • Cross-docking

  • Labeling and packaging

  • Order fulfillment

  • Reverse logistics

Partnering with a provider that offers integrated logistics solutions can improve operational efficiency and reduce overall supply chain complexity.

For example, businesses can benefit from combining warehousing with freight forwarding, customs clearance, and transportation services through a single logistics provider.

Learn more about integrated logistics solutions at Globeflight Kenya's Warehousing Services page: https://www.globeflight.co.ke/

7. Analyze Cost Transparency and Customer Support

While pricing is an important consideration, the lowest-cost option is not always the best choice.

Businesses should seek warehousing providers that offer transparent pricing structures and clearly communicate all associated costs.

Evaluate factors such as:

  • Storage fees

  • Handling charges

  • Fulfillment costs

  • Transportation expenses

  • Contract flexibility

In addition, strong customer support is essential. Your warehousing partner should provide responsive communication, proactive problem-solving, and regular performance updates.

A reliable logistics partner becomes an extension of your business and contributes directly to customer satisfaction.

Why Choosing the Right Warehousing Partner Matters

An effective warehousing partner does more than store inventory. They help businesses:

  • Improve inventory accuracy

  • Reduce operating costs

  • Enhance customer satisfaction

  • Increase order fulfillment speed

  • Support business growth

  • Improve supply chain visibility

As supply chains become increasingly complex, businesses must prioritize partnerships that contribute to long-term operational success.

The right warehouse provider can become a strategic asset that enables businesses to remain competitive in evolving markets.

Best Practices for Successful Warehouse Partnerships

Once you've selected a warehousing partner, consider these best practices:

  • Establish clear service expectations

  • Monitor key performance indicators (KPIs)

  • Conduct regular inventory audits

  • Maintain open communication

  • Review warehouse performance regularly

  • Plan for future growth requirements

Strong collaboration between businesses and warehousing providers leads to improved efficiency and long-term success.

Conclusion

Choosing the right warehousing partner is one of the most important decisions a business can make. A reliable provider supports inventory management, improves operational efficiency, reduces costs, and strengthens overall supply chain performance.

By carefully evaluating location, scalability, technology, security, industry expertise, value-added services, and customer support, businesses can identify a warehousing partner that aligns with their operational goals and growth strategy.

At Globeflight Kenya, we understand the critical role warehousing plays in modern logistics. Our comprehensive logistics and supply chain solutions are designed to help businesses optimize inventory management, improve efficiency, and support sustainable growth.

To learn more about professional warehousing and logistics solutions, visit https://www.globeflight.co.ke/.

External Resources

For additional information on warehousing and supply chain best practices, consider these resources:

  • Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals (CSCMP): https://cscmp.org

  • World Trade Organization Logistics Resources: https://www.wto.org

  • International Warehouse Logistics Association (IWLA): https://www.iwla.com

Investing time in selecting the right warehousing partner today can create lasting benefits for your business tomorrow.

blogs.content:
Are you a foreign business looking to ship goods into Kenya without setting up a local company? Or perhaps you are an enterprise struggling with Kenya's complex customs regulations and compliance requirements? If so, you need an Importer of Record (IOR) — and understanding how this service works could save your business significant time, money, and legal risk.

In this guide, Globeflight Kenya walks you through everything you need to know about Importer of Record services in Kenya: what it means, why it matters, and how to choose the right IOR partner for your business.

What Is an Importer of Record (IOR)?

An Importer of Record is the individual or business entity that is legally responsible for ensuring that imported goods comply with all local laws, regulations, and customs requirements at the point of entry into a country.

In Kenya, the Importer of Record assumes full legal accountability for:

  • Accurate customs documentation and declarations

  • Payment of import duties, VAT, and applicable levies

  • Compliance with Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) requirements

  • Obtaining necessary permits, certifications, and licences

  • Ensuring goods meet Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) regulations

Simply put, the IOR is the entity that "signs off" on your shipment in the eyes of Kenyan customs authorities. Without a recognised Importer of Record, your goods cannot legally enter the country.

Why Do Businesses in Kenya Need an Importer of Record?

Many foreign companies and even local businesses underestimate how complex importing into Kenya can be. Kenya has one of the most structured — yet demanding — import regulatory environments in East Africa.

Here is why an IOR is not just helpful, but often essential:

1. You Do Not Have a Registered Local Entity

To act as your own Importer of Record in Kenya, your business must be legally registered in the country. Most international companies shipping goods to Kenya — whether IT equipment, medical devices, industrial machinery, or consumer goods — do not have a local subsidiary. In this case, appointing a professional IOR service provider like Globeflight Kenya is the only compliant option.

2. Kenya's Import Regulations Are Strict

Importing into Kenya requires navigating multiple layers of regulation. Goods must comply with KEBS standards, and most product categories require a Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) certificate and a Certificate of Conformity (CoC) before they can clear customs. Failure to meet these requirements leads to shipment delays, penalties, or even seizure of goods.

3. Complex Tax and Duty Structure

Kenya applies a layered taxation system on imports, which includes:

  • Import Duty: 0% to 25% depending on the product category

  • Value Added Tax (VAT): 16%, calculated on the CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight) value plus applicable duties

  • Import Declaration Fee (IDF): 3.5% of the customs value

  • Railway Development Levy (RDL): 2% of the customs value

Incorrect valuation or misclassification of goods can trigger customs reviews, financial penalties, and significant delays. An experienced IOR ensures everything is correctly declared from the start.

4. Industry-Specific Requirements

Certain sectors face additional regulatory scrutiny in Kenya:

  • IT and Telecommunications Equipment: Must obtain an Import Standardisation Mark (ISM) certificate from KEBS

The Step-by-Step Clearance Workflow

The process begins with the formal declaration of goods through the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) online system. Once the declaration is submitted, the system assesses the applicable taxes and duties based on the nature of your shipment. This digital transition has made Customs Clearance in Kenya much more transparent than in previous years.

After the assessment, your cargo may undergo physical or documentary verification by customs officers. If everything aligns with your submitted paperwork, the system generates a release order. This final step allows your goods to be cleared for transport to your final destination, marking the successful end of the import cycle.

Breakdown of Import Duties and Levies

Most import costs are calculated based on the Cost, Insurance, and Freight (CIF) value of your goods. This total represents the price of the items, the cost of shipping, and the insurance premiums paid to get the cargo to a Kenyan port. Once the CIF value is established, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) applies several standard charges.

You should prepare for the following primary financial obligations:

  • Import Duty: This is a percentage-based tax that varies depending on the type of goods you are importing.

  • Value Added Tax (VAT): A standard tax applied to the sum of the CIF value and the import duty.

  • Railway Development Levy (RDL): A specific fee dedicated to the development of railway infrastructure in the country.

blogs.content:
In logistics, we usually worry about what we can see: lead times, fuel prices, and port congestion. But starting May 1, 2026, the industry is shifting its focus to something invisible: radiation security.

The Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority (KNRA) recently issued a directive that will change the workflow for every importer and exporter in the country. From next month, every single container inbound or outbound must undergo mandatory nuclear screening.

Why the Change?

This isn’t just another layer of bureaucracy. As Kenya moves closer to its goal of a 2,000 MW nuclear power plant, our national security framework is evolving to meet international (IAEA) standards. By installing Radiation Portal Monitors (RPMs) at the Port of Mombasa and our ICDs.

It’s a "pre-emptive strike" against the illicit movement of radioactive materials, and while it adds a new step to the process, it’s a necessary one for a country with nuclear ambitions.

The Operational Reality: What Shippers Need to Know

For the supply chains, "mandatory" usually triggers one word: Delays. However, the transition doesn’t have to be painful if we are proactive. Here is what to watch closely:

  • HS Code Precision: The KNRA has been very clear incorrect codes on manifests will be the first ones flagged for manual verification. In an era of automated scanning, "close enough" is no longer good enough for your HS codes.

  • Legal Notice 160: Updating the billing templates to reflect the new specialized verification fees. Transparency with clients now will prevent "invoice shock" in June.

  • The Adjustment Period: New traffic flows at the port will inevitably lead to some "teething problems" in the first two weeks of May. We are advising our partners to build a small buffer into their time-sensitive deliveries during this transition.

The question for our industry isn't whether we can afford the extra few minutes of screening; it’s whether we can afford the risk of not having it as we enter the nuclear age.

Between February 28 and March 1, 2026, a joint military strike by the United States and Israel targeted sites in Iran, prompting swift retaliatory actions by Iran directed at U.S. bases and interests in the region.

While the direct military exchanges remain geographically contained within the Middle East for the time being, the repercussions for international transportation and supply chains are already immediate, widespread, and profound.

Key Developments Driving the Disruption

  • Airfreight Operations Grounded: Major airports and airspace across the Gulf region (including key hubs in Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and beyond) have faced closures or severe restrictions. Airlines have suspended flights to, from, and over the affected areas, invoking force majeure in many cases. This has created instant backlogs and forced rerouting of cargo, significantly tightening global air capacity.

  • Ocean Freight Routes Under Pressure: The strategic Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for roughly 20-30% of the world's oil and a vital artery for container and bulk shipments, has seen partial or threatened closures, heightening navigation risks. Combined with ongoing regional instability (including prior Red Sea challenges), many carriers have reverted to or maintained longer Cape of Good Hope routings, erasing recent tentative gains in Suez Canal usage.

  • Broader Ripple Effects: Regional airspace shutdowns, port delays, and increased security protocols are compounding into shipment backlogs, longer transit times, rate volatility, and higher insurance premiums across ocean, air, and multimodal lanes.

The situation remains extremely fluid, with the potential for rapid changes in military posture, diplomatic interventions, or further retaliatory measures. Logistics providers, shippers, and forwarders must treat this as a high-volatility environment where plans can shift within hours.

Short-Term Implications for Global Supply Chains

  • Capacity Constraints: Expect reduced lift on key Asia–Europe, Asia–Middle East, and transatlantic routes due to reroutings and suspensions.

  • Cost Increases: Spot rates are likely to spike in response to scarcity, with estimates from industry sources suggesting 20-30% uplifts in affected corridors. War risk and kidnap & ransom (K&R) insurance add further premiums.

  • Transit Time Extensions: What were recently shortened lead times (via partial Suez returns) have reversed, pushing delays of 7+ days on some loops.

  • Congestion Risks: Alternative gateways and ports may face secondary overload as volumes shift.

Recommendations for Businesses

Globeflight and similar providers are actively monitoring developments 24/7, reviewing contingency plans, and communicating lane-specific advisories to clients. In the current environment:

  • Build in buffer stock where feasible.

  • Explore multimodal alternatives.

  • Discuss risk mitigation, rerouting options, and insurance adjustments with your logistics partner immediately.

  • Stay informed through trusted industry sources, as the picture evolves quickly.

Global trade has proven resilient through repeated disruptions, but the current escalation underscores the fragility of key arteries like the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf airspace. Vigilance, flexibility, and proactive planning remain essential to safeguarding supply chain continuity.

blogs.title: Logistics Distribution 101: What Exactly Is Distribution Logistics?
blogs.shortDescription: In today's fast-moving world of e-commerce, retail, and global trade, products rarely go straight from factory to shopper.
