blogs.content:
In today's fast-moving world of e-commerce, retail, and global trade, products rarely go straight from factory to shopper. Something crucial happens in between: distribution logistics. Also called outbound logistics or sales logistics, this is the part of the supply chain that bridges production and the end customer. Simply put, distribution logistics handles everything needed to move finished goods from warehouses or distribution centers to retailers, businesses, or directly to consumers as quickly, accurately, and cost-effectively as possible.

What Exactly Is Distribution Logistics?

Distribution logistics focuses on the outbound flow of products after manufacturing or assembly is complete. It includes planning, executing, and controlling the physical movement and storage of goods so they reach the right place at the right time.

Key definition: Distribution logistics = the sum of processes that get products from a company's facilities (warehouse, DC, or plant) to the final customer.

It differs slightly from broader logistics (which covers the entire supply chain, including inbound raw materials) and from pure transportation (which is just one piece moving stuff from A to B). Distribution logistics is more execution-oriented: it's about making sure the product is available where and when the customer expects it.

Core goals of distribution logistics:

  • Minimize delivery time (speed)

  • Reduce costs (transport, storage, handling)

  • Maximize reliability (on-time, damage-free delivery)

  • Improve customer satisfaction

Main Components of Distribution Logistics

Distribution logistics involves several interconnected activities. Here's a breakdown of the essentials:

  1. Order Processing The journey starts when a customer (or retailer) places an order. This includes order entry, validation, invoicing, and preparing picking lists. Modern systems use warehouse management software (WMS) to automate this step.

  2. Warehousing & Storage Goods are held in distribution centers (DCs), regional warehouses, or fulfillment centers. Key decisions include the following: Location of warehouses (closer to customers = faster delivery but higher cost) Layout and slotting (placing fast-moving items near packing areas) Storage types (pallet racking, shelving, automated systems)

  3. Inventory Management Maintaining the right stock levels is critical. Too much inventory ties up capital and increases storage costs; too little leads to stockouts and lost sales. Techniques include ABC analysis, just-in-time (JIT), and safety stock calculations.

  4. Picking & Packing Workers pick items from shelves based on orders, then pack them securely. Accuracy here prevents returns and complaints. Technologies like pick-to-light, voice picking, or automated guided vehicles (AGVs) boost efficiency.

  5. Transportation & Routing This is the visible part: trucks, vans, ships, planes, or even couriers for the last mile. Key choices: Mode (road, air, sea) Carrier selection (own fleet vs. third-party) Route optimization (using software to minimize distance/fuel)

  6. Last-Mile Delivery The final leg is from the local hub to the customer's door. Often the most expensive and complex part due to urban traffic, failed deliveries, and customer expectations for same-day or next-day service.

  7. Returns Management (Reverse Logistics) Handling returns, refunds, inspections, and restocking. Efficient reverse logistics turns potential losses into recovered value.

Common Distribution Models

Businesses choose different structures depending on their products, customers, and scale:

  • Direct Distribution — Manufacturer → Customer

  • Indirect Distribution — Manufacturer → Wholesaler/Distributor → Retailer → Customer

  • E-commerce Fulfillment — Seller → 3PL warehouse → Customer

  • Hub-and-Spoke—A central hub feeds regional spokes for faster local delivery

  • Cross-Docking—Goods move directly from inbound to outbound trucks with minimal storage

Why Distribution Logistics Matters in 2026

Customers now expect Amazon-level speed and transparency everywhere. Poor distribution leads to:

  • Lost sales from delays/stockouts

  • Higher costs from rush shipping or excess inventory

  • Damaged brand reputation from late or wrong deliveries

Good distribution logistics delivers a competitive advantage through the following:

  • Lower total delivered cost

  • Higher on-time delivery rates

  • Better cash flow

  • Scalability during peaks seasons

Quick Tips

  • Start with data: Track key metrics like order cycle time, perfect order rate, transportation cost per unit, and inventory turnover.

  • Embrace technology: WMS, TMS (transportation management systems), and route optimization software pay off quickly.

  • Consider outsourcing: Many companies use 3PL providers for warehousing and distribution to avoid heavy capital investment.

  • Focus on sustainability: Customers and regulations increasingly favor green logistics (electric vans, optimized routes to cut emissions).

Distribution logistics may seem like "just moving boxes," but it's a strategic powerhouse. Master the basics and you'll understand why some companies deliver in hours while others take days.

Whether you're running a small online store in Nairobi or managing a multinational supply chain, strong distribution logistics turns promises into satisfied customers, one delivery at a time.

  • Shipments shipped from 9 February 2026 without a Certificate of Conformity (CoC) will undergo destination inspection.

  • Importers will pay an inspection fee equivalent to 0.6% of the customs value

  • KEBS is procuring new inspection companies; services will resume after the process is completed

KEBS recommends importers take proactive compliance measures:

1. Product Testing Before Shipment

Importers should obtain Kenyan standards and have products tested in ISO/IEC 17025 accredited laboratories before shipping.

2. Product Registration / Diamond Mark

Registering products under KEBS certification schemes ensures smoother clearance and reduced inspection risks.

3. Pre-Arrival Documentation

Submit required compliance documents through the National Single Window System before cargo arrival.

Special Notice

Imports from EAC partner states continue under regional standards frameworks, and used motor vehicle inspections remain handled separately under existing arrangements.

blogs.title: Naivasha depot operationalised to decongest Port of Mombasa
blogs.shortDescription:
The government has activated the Naivasha Inland Container Depot as a key clearance hub for transit cargo to ease congestion at the Port of Mombasa.
South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, and the DRC are set to begin operations at the facility as cargo volumes at Mombasa continue to rise.
blogs.content:
For years, the Port of Mombasa has been the undisputed gateway to East Africa. However, success has brought its own set of challenges: chronic congestion, rising costs, and a logistics chain stretched to its breaking point. In a strategic pivot, the Kenyan government has officially moved to operationalize the Naivasha Inland Container Depot (ICD) as the primary clearance hub for regional transit goods.

The Numbers: Why Now?

The urgency behind this move is driven by record-breaking cargo volumes. In 2025, Mombasa Port handled 45.45 million metric tons, a significant leap from 40.99 million in 2024.

This surge, partly fueled by regional geopolitical shifts that saw traders rerouting shipments through Kenya for stability, pushed port infrastructure to its limits. While Mombasa was overflowing, the Naivasha ICD, with a capacity of 4,000 TEUs, sat largely underutilized at just 19% occupancy.

A Regional Clearing House

KRA Commissioner General Humphrey Wattanga has made the strategy clear: Naivasha is now the priority for long-haul cargo. * Transit Destinations: Goods bound for Uganda, Rwanda, the DRC, and South Sudan will now be cleared at Naivasha.

  • Mombasa Focus: The coastal port will pivot to focus primarily on domestic and short-haul traffic.

“The utilization of Naivasha ICD will reduce congestion at the port, lower clearance timelines, and cut transport costs for regional traders,” Humphrey Wattanga, KRA Commissioner General.

South Sudan Takes the Lead

Perhaps the most tangible sign of this shift is the official handover of 10 acres of land within the Naivasha Special Economic Zone (SEZ) to the government of South Sudan.

South Sudan Revenue Authority (SSRA) Commissioner General William Kuol has confirmed that Juba plans to have its own cargo clearance facility operational at the site within the next five months. With South Sudan accounting for 12.7% of transit cargo through Mombasa, this "dry port" will offer a faster, more predictable route for Juba’s importers.

The Broader Vision: 6,000 Acres of Opportunity

The Naivasha ICD is just one piece of a much larger puzzle. The surrounding Special Economic Zone (SEZ) spans 6,000 acres and has already attracted 20 major investors.

  • Land Allocations: Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and the DRC have also been allocated land for national cargo handling stations.

  • Infrastructure: Massive works are underway to ensure road networks and power connectivity are ready to support these regional hubs.

SGR Extension

To fully realize this potential, the government is in final talks to extend the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) from Naivasha through Kisumu to the Malaba border. This extension will create a seamless, high-capacity rail link from the Indian Ocean deep into the hinterlands of East Africa.

blogs.title: KRA & KPA Joint Reforms to Decongest Mombasa Port
blogs.shortDescription:
To eliminate operational bottlenecks, reduce cargo dwell time, and strengthen Kenya’s competitiveness as East Africa's premier logistics hub.

The Kenya Port Authority and the Kenya Revenue Authority have rolled out a "strategic reset" focused on seven key areas to accelerate cargo clearance and improve efficiency along the Northern Corridor.
blogs.content:
1. Evacuation of Long-Stay Cargo (21+ Days)

To immediately free up critical yard space, a strict timeline has been imposed on cargo storage.

  • The Reform: All domestic and transit cargo that has remained at the port for more than 21 days is now classified as "long-stay."

  • Action: These containers will be compulsorily transferred from the port’s G-Section to designated Container Freight Stations (CFSs) and Inland Container Depots (ICDs).

  • Impact: This rapid evacuation prevents yard clogging, allowing faster offloading of new vessels and reducing ship turnaround time.

2. Expanded Pre-Arrival Processing (PAP)

KRA is shifting from a "clearance after arrival" model to a more efficient "clearance before arrival" framework.

  • The Reform: The Pre-Arrival Processing (PAP) framework is being expanded significantly.

  • Target Cargo: Priority is given to bulk cargo, low-risk shipments, and goods belonging to Authorized Economic Operators (AEOs).

  • Impact: By processing customs documents and payments while the ship is still at sea, cargo can be released almost immediately upon docking, increasing predictability for traders.

3. Multi-Vendor RECTS Seal System

To fix delays caused by the shortage of electronic seals for transit goods, the supply chain for tracking devices is being liberalized.

  • The Reform: KRA is moving away from a single-vendor system to a multi-vendor model for the Regional Electronic Cargo Tracking System (RECTS).

  • Action: An open "expression of interest" process will allow multiple vetted vendors to supply the electronic seals.

  • Impact: This ensures a steady supply of seals, eliminating the "waiting time" for transit trucks. It guarantees uninterrupted tracking of goods destined for Uganda, Rwanda, South Sudan, and DRC.

4. Increased SGR Wagons to Inland Depots

A multimodal approach is being used to speed up the movement of freight from the coast to the hinterland.

  • The Reform: KRA and KPA have engaged the Kenya Railways Corporation to deploy additional freight wagons on the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR).

  • Action: High-frequency rail transfers will move cargo directly from Mombasa to the Embakasi (Nairobi) and Naivasha Inland Container Depots.

  • Impact: This reduces reliance on road transport for the initial leg of the journey, decreases road congestion, and ensures faster delivery to importers in Nairobi and transit markets.

5. Lamu Port Transhipment Boost

The reforms strategically utilize the Port of Lamu to offload pressure from Mombasa.

  • The Reform: A deliberate shift to increase the utilization of Lamu Port for transhipment cargo (goods moved from one ship to another for final delivery elsewhere).

  • Action: KPA has committed dedicated infrastructure and operational resources at Lamu to handle this specific traffic.

  • Impact: By diverting transhipment activity to Lamu, the Port of Mombasa (Kilindini) can focus more efficiently on domestic and direct transit imports.

6. Dedicated Empty Container Management

One of the biggest causes of congestion is the accumulation of empty containers waiting to be returned to shipping lines.

  • The Reform: KPA has allocated a specific site within the port solely for the stacking and loading of empty containers.

  • Action: A new industry framework for empty container management (effective late January 2026) has been established to improve coordination between shipping lines and transporters.

  • Impact: This organizes the chaotic flow of returning empties, ensuring they don't block the entry and exit of loaded trucks.

7. Enhanced Digital Integration

The backbone of these physical reforms is a digital upgrade to cut red tape.

  • The Reform: Deeper integration of KRA’s iCMS (Integrated Customs Management System) and KPA’s KWATOS (Kilindini Waterfront Automated Terminal Operations System).

  • Action: The goal is to eliminate multiple documentation requirements and manual interventions.

  • Impact: A seamless digital handshake between agencies means data is shared in real-time, reducing "human error" and opportunities for corruption while speeding up the release process.

blogs.title: KPA Effects New Cargo Handling Fees
blogs.shortDescription: The Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) officially began implementing its new port tariff structure on Monday, December 22, ending a three-month delay that had pushed back the rollout from the original effective date of September 15.
blogs.content:
In the KPA Tariff Book 2025, costs for key services have risen significantly, affecting almost every stage of port operations, from vessel docking and cargo handling to storage and licensing.

According to the KPA, “the new rates are meant to reflect current operational realities and finance ongoing modernization projects, including digital transformation, infrastructure upgrades, and green port initiatives.”

Under the new charges, annual business license fees have increased significantly, with specialized cargo providers now required to pay Ksh2.3 million, while truck operators handling water or bunkers will pay Ksh1.5 million each year. However, small service providers, such as weighing or bagging service providers, will part with Ksh 1.05 million each year.

These new annual license fees are a significant increase from under Ksh300,000, which had remained constant for a decade. The higher costs are a burden that small traders state would push them out of the market. 

At the same time, cargo storage charges have been raised significantly. Under the new structure, an imported container left beyond the free storage period will now incur a daily charge of between Ksh 9,000 and 15,000. For dangerous cargo, the daily rate for container storage has been set at Ksh 12,000, up from Ksh 6,000, which was KPA’s initial charge. 

For shipping lines and vessel operators, tug and salvage services will now cost between Ksh450,000 and Ksh750,000, while mobile crane hire ranges from Ksh150,000 to Ksh300,000 per hour. Forklifts and tractors will cost up to Ksh67,000 per hour.

The revised penalties also introduce new fines for late or incorrect documentation. Exporters submitting cargo late will be charged Ksh15,000 per container. Additionally, any change in cargo destination (as indicated on the C-11 form) will incur a fine of Ksh15,000 per bill of lading.

Additionally, bulk importers of cement, steel, tiles, and paint will face higher prices as port handling charges for these materials increase by 20–30 percent.

KPA explained that the delay in implementing the new tariff was prompted by extended stakeholder consultations, a court challenge by freight associations, and the need for system upgrades to integrate the new billing model at Mombasa and Lamu ports. 

Concerned, importers and transporters say the changes will deepen the cost-of-living crisis by increasing freight and logistics expenses, while clearing agents in Mombasa argue that demurrage and documentation penalties will likely be passed on to consumers.

Moreover, truck operators warn that higher licensing and storage fees will drive up retail prices nationwide.

blogs.title: Kenya’s Motor Import Guide: Every Regulation, Tax, and Loophole Explained.
blogs.shortDescription: If you are planning to import a vehicle into Kenya, the rules have changed. The 2018 age limit is closing fast, 'Certificate of Origin' is now mandatory, and the tax man is watching every invoice. You can't afford to guess anymore; you need a strategy and the right partner. Find out more.
blogs.content:
Let’s be honest: Importing a vehicle into Kenya right now feels less like a business transaction and more like an extreme sport.

Between the KRA’s shifting valuation systems (CRSP), the 8-year age limit ticking clock, and duties that can literally double the price of your car, many aspiring car owners and dealers are drowning in paperwork and unexpected costs.

But here is the truth: Despite the chaos, the opportunities are massive if you know the rules. Whether you are eyeing a Toyota vehicle from Japan, a heavy commercial truck from the UK, or an electric vehicle (EV), you need a strategy, not just a wish list.

Before you spend a shilling, know who you are dealing with. If you annoy one, your car stays at the port.

  1. KRA: They decide what your car is worth. Currently, there is a battle over the CRSP (Current Retail Selling Price).

  2. KEBS: They enforce the KS 1515:2000 standard. If your car is older than 8 years or isn't right-hand drive? It gets crushed or sent back at your cost.

  3. NTSA (The Registrar): No NTSA clearance, no number plates, no logbook.

  4. KenTrade: The digital doorway for all your Import Declaration Forms (IDF).

How Much Will You Actually Pay?

The biggest shock for importers is the cumulative tax. It’s not just one fee; it’s a tax on top of a tax.

The "Painful" Reality (Standard Combustion Engine)

Scenario: Importing a 2022 Toyota Corolla (1800 cc)

  • Import Duty (25% of CIF): 0.25 × 2,500,000 = KES 625,000

  • Excise Duty (25% of CIF + Import Duty): 0.25 × (2,500,000 + 625,000) = 0.25 × 3,125,000 = KES 781,250

  • VAT (16% of CIF + Import Duty + Excise Duty): 0.16 × (2,500,000 + 625,000 + 781,250) = 0.16 × 3,906,250 = KES 625,000

  • IDF + RDL (3.5% + 2% = 5.5% of CIF): 0.055 × 2,500,000 = KES 137,500

  • Total Taxes: 625,000 + 781,250 + 625,000 + 137,500 = KES 2,168,750

  • Final Cost to You (CIF + Taxes): 2,500,000 + 2,168,750 = KES 4,668,750

The Electric Vehicles

Scenario: Importing a 2023 Tesla Model 3

  • CIF value of KES 4,000,000 (approx. USD 30,500 at current rates; common for a used 2023 Model 3, including cost, insurance, and freight):

  • Import Duty: 0% × KES 4M = KES 0

  • Excise Duty: 10% × KES 4M = KES 400,000

  • VAT: 0% (exempt) × (KES 4M + KES 400K) = KES 0

  • IDF + RDL: 5.5% × KES 4M = KES 220,000

  • Total Taxes: KES 620,000 (15.5% effective rate)

  • Final Cost to You: KES 4M (CIF) + KES 620K (taxes) + KES 100K (misc. fees like inspection/agent) = KES 4,720,000

3 Hidden Traps Catching Importers in 2025

1. The "Certificate of Origin" Nightmare

Since July 2025, if you don't have a valid Certificate of Origin (COO) from the exporting country, KRA will stall your clearance. We’ve seen cars stuck at Mombasa for weeks because of this single paper.

2. The "Age Limit"

Kenya has a strict 8-year age limit. 2

  • The Rule: You cannot import a car manufactured before 2018 right now.

  • The Warning: There is chatter about tightening this to 7 years starting Jan 2026.

3. The Valuation War (CRSP)

KRA has been pushing to raise the CRSP (the "book value" they use to tax you). While courts have paused some hikes, using an inexperienced clearing agent who uses old rates can lead to massive "uplifts" (tax penalties) when the car arrives.

How to Import Without the Headache

You can try to fight the KRA, coordinate the PVoC inspection in Japan, and argue with NTSA yourself. Or, you can let Globeflight Worldwide Express handle it.

We don't just "clear" goods; we engineer the import process to save you money.

Why Smart Importers Choose Globeflight:

  • Pre-Compliance Audit: We check your vehicle's age, specs, and paperwork before you pay the supplier.

  • Tax Optimization: We know the latest legal notices (especially for EVs and hybrids) to ensure you pay the legal minimum tax, not a penny more.

  • Speed: We clear faster because our documentation is perfect. No demurrage (storage fees) eating your profit.

  • Door-to-Door: From the auction floor in Tokyo/UK/Dubai to your driveway in Nairobi.

Conclusion: Don't Gamble with Your Capital

The motor industry in Kenya is lucrative, but it is unforgiving. One missing document or one wrong calculation can cost you hundreds of thousands of shillings.

blogs.title: South Sudan imports affected as Kenyan clearing agents halt services over fees
blogs.shortDescription: Trade Crisis at Mombasa Port: Kenyan clearing agents have indefinitely suspended services for all cargo destined for South Sudan. The boycott is a protest against a sudden $3,580 fee per container imposed by Juba, leaving essential goods stranded and threatening severe supply chain disruptions for the landlocked nation.
blogs.content:
South Sudan Imports Paralyzed as Agents Protest New Fees

The Situation A significant trade standoff has erupted at the Port of Mombasa, effectively freezing the flow of goods into South Sudan. Kenyan clearing and forwarding agents have officially halted all services for cargo bound for Juba, citing an "irregular and punitive" new levy introduced by the South Sudan Revenue Authority (SSRA).

The Cause: A Surprise $3,580 Charge The core of the dispute is a new directive from the SSRA requiring a $3,580 (approx. KES 460,000) payment per container.

  • The Levy: The fee is ostensibly for a "Maritime Container Release One-Time Password (OTP)," which the South Sudanese government claims is necessary for better cargo tracking and accountability.

  • The Problem: Agents argue this fee was introduced without any consultation or official diplomatic engagement. Roy Mwanthi, a representative for the agents, stated that the directive appeared via social media rather than official trade channels, violating East African Community (EAC) protocols.

The Container Deposit Controversy Complicating matters further, the SSRA simultaneously abolished the traditional $5,000 container deposit fee.

  • While this might seem like a relief for traders, agents view it as a massive liability.

  • The deposit previously acted as insurance, ensuring that containers were returned to shipping lines after delivery in South Sudan. Without it, agents fear they will be held financially responsible for lost or unreturned containers, a common issue in the region.

The Impact The suspension of services has immediate and severe consequences:

  • Stranded Cargo: Hundreds of containers carrying food, fuel, and general merchandise are now stuck at the Port of Mombasa and Container Freight Stations (CFSs).

  • Supply Chain Shock: As a landlocked country, South Sudan relies on the Mombasa port for the vast majority of its imports. A prolonged strike could lead to shortages of essential commodities and price hikes in Juba.

  • Stalemate: Agents have vowed not to resume work until the $3,580 fee is scrapped and proper consultations are held, while the SSRA maintains the measure is needed to curb tax evasion.

Next Steps for Traders If you are moving cargo to South Sudan, expect significant delays. It is advisable to halt new bookings until the Kenya International Freight and Warehousing Association (KIFWA) and the South Sudanese government resolve the impasse.

blogs.shortDescription: The global supply chain is increasingly defined by data and digital integration. In a major move to solidify East Africa's place in the digital trade economy, DP World has rolled out its advanced Port Community System (PCS) in Kenya. Focusing on the critical Port of Mombasa, this ambitious project is not just an upgrade; it's a foundational transformation expected to revolutionize the speed, transparency, and efficiency of trade across the entire region.
blogs.content:
1. What is the Port Community System (PCS)? The Port Community System is a neutral, open, and electronic platform that interconnects the disparate information technology systems operated by various public and private organizations in the port and logistics community. Essentially, it acts as a single, centralized "digital nerve center" for the entire trade ecosystem.

The CARGOES Ecosystem The PCS implemented in Mombasa is part of DP World's proprietary CARGOES platform, a digital suite designed to streamline global logistics. Crucially, the system was developed in collaboration with EMEA Port Logistics and implemented alongside the Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) and the Government of Kenya.

It is important to note that DP World provides the technology but does not operate the Port of Mombasa. The system is designed to provide seamless digital tools for all users, regardless of who manages the physical terminal operations.

  1. Key Features and Digital Tools for Users The PCS replaces multiple manual, paper-based, or siloed electronic processes with a single, unified digital interface. It serves a broad range of stakeholders, including importers, exporters, freight forwarders, transport companies, customs agents, and various government agencies.

The system offers a comprehensive suite of digital tools, which can be summarized as follows:

Cargo Tracking and Visibility:

The system provides real-time, end-to-end status updates on cargo movements from vessel arrival to gate exit, which allows traders to anticipate delivery, reduce uncertainty, and lower planning costs.

Gate Booking:

It facilitates the scheduling of truck movements for cargo pick-up and drop-off, effectively cutting down on gate congestion, reducing vehicle idling time, and significantly improving port throughput.

Digital Billing and Payments:

All invoicing is centralized, and electronic settlement of port and associated charges is enabled, which increases financial transparency and speeds up the entire clearance chain.

Real-Time Status Updates:

Users receive immediate notifications regarding customs clearance, inspections, and documentation status, thereby minimizing manual follow-ups and bureaucratic delays.

CARGOES Customs Integration:

The PCS connects directly with Kenya’s eCitizen platform, facilitating digital customs declarations and AI-enabled risk management to enhance compliance and drastically reduce physical interventions.

Enhances customs compliance and drastically reduces physical interventions.

  1. The Transformative Impact on Kenya’s Trade The Port of Mombasa is not just Kenya's port; it is the vital maritime gateway for over a dozen landlocked nations, including Uganda, Rwanda, South Sudan, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The efficiency of Mombasa directly affects the economies of the entire East and Central Africa region.

Efficiency and Speed 30% Reduction in Clearance Time: The most frequently cited benefit is the expected reduction of cargo clearance times by up to 30% once the system is fully operational. This is a massive saving in operational cost and time-to-market for goods.

Reduced Dwell Time: The PCS enables the Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) to manage gate operations and cargo stacking more intelligently, leading to significantly shorter dwell times (the duration a container stays in the terminal).

Benefit to 3,000+ Users: Over 3,000 port users annually are expected to benefit from faster turnaround times.

Transparency and Governance Single Window Operations: By integrating public and private sector systems, the PCS minimizes opportunities for corruption and manual document manipulation, creating a more transparent environment.

Data-Driven Decision Making: The system generates massive amounts of high-quality data. KPA and other government agencies can use this data for smarter planning, risk assessment (especially through the AI-enabled customs platform), and optimization of operational resources.

Economic and Strategic Importance The introduction of the PCS aligns perfectly with Kenya's Vision 2030 goal of modernizing infrastructure and transitioning to a digitally enabled economy. By improving logistics capabilities, Kenya strengthens its position as the premier maritime hub for East Africa, boosting its competitiveness against other regional ports.

As DP World's Chief Operating Officer of Digital Trade Solutions stated, "Digitization is no longer optional; it is essential for unlocking the full potential of African trade." This platform connects Mombasa not just to the global shipping lanes but fully to the digital global trade economy.

  1. Conclusion: A New Benchmark for African Trade The deployment of the DP World Port Community System in Mombasa marks a pivotal moment in the digitalization of African trade corridors. For the average Kenyan, this means a more efficient flow of goods, potentially leading to lower costs for imports and faster access to international markets for exports. For businesses and government, it offers unparalleled transparency and operational control. The success of the Mombasa PCS is set to become a new regional benchmark for digital integration, driving wider adoption of similar technologies across Africa and ensuring that the continent remains competitive in the rapidly evolving landscape of global logistics.

blogs.title: Kenya digitizes customs at Busia Border to seal revenue leaks
blogs.shortDescription: KRA Commissioner of Customs and Border Control, Lilian Nyawanda,described the app as a tool designed to simplify tax payments, strengthen monitoring, and make trade easier especially for small-scale traders who have long complained of slow and cumbersome procedures
blogs.content:
Busia, Monday 24 November 2025 - A smart digital solution to simplify trade, speed up clearance of goods, and modernise border operations has been launched today in Kenya, as part of a 15-year partnership to accelerate trade growth across the country’s borders.

Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), in collaboration with TradeMark Africa (TMA) and the British High Commission (BHC), has launched the eCUSTOMS app at the Busia One Stop Border Post (OSBP) on the Kenya-Uganda border. This new platform is designed to make customs declarations faster, paperless, and hassle-free for traders, transporters, and passengers.

The eCUSTOMS app is a game-changer for Kenya and East Africa’s trade facilitation efforts. It aims to cut down clearance time at borders, boost transparency and compliance with regional customs laws, support SMEs (Small to Medium Enterprises) and transporters with easy-to-use digital tools, and strengthen Kenya’s position as a leader in modern, secure, and efficient border management.

The new app will save time and money. It will reduce cumulative truck waiting time by 1,200 hours daily at the Busia OSBP (about one hour per truck) will also save small traders approximately KES 750 per customs declaration – modest from a corporate perspective, but for a woman crossing the border twice per day, it’s the difference between profit and loss.

This is the latest milestone in the 15-year partnership in Kenya between the UK, TMA and KRA to turbocharge cross border trade. In 2018, border clearance time was reduced by at least 79% between Uganda and Kenya after the construction and operationalisation of the Busia OSBP, whilst government revenues substantially increased.

The Regional Electronic Cargo Tracking System (RECTS) has significantly enhanced cargo movement efficiency, reducing transit time from Mombasa to Busia from 15 days to 2.9 days, and from 15 days to 3.1 days on the Mombasa–Malaba route between 2024 and 2025.[1]  For every $1 invested in the system, the Integrated Cargo Management System (iCMS) has generated $838 in returns; $570 from customs duties and $267 from other taxes.

Humphrey Wattanga, Commissioner General, KRA, said:

eCUSTOMS will ease cross-border trade and promote a conducive business environment by simplifying customs declarations and modernizing border operations. By enabling paperless and seamless processes, this platform will provide traders with faster, more accessible, and more transparent services. KRA remains committed to continued investment in technology to ensure our processes remain as efficient and user-friendly as possible.

H.E Hailemariam Boshe, Former Prime Minister of Ethiopia and TMA Board Chair, said:

This is a major milestone for integrating trade across East Africa. The more trade we can do across our borders, the more we can grow together. This launch shows how technology and partnerships can unlock regional economic growth.

Dr. Ed Barnett MBE, Chargé d’Affaires, British High Commission Nairobi, said:

This long-term partnership has delivered a solution directly into the hands of small businesses – the hustling backbone of Kenya’s economy. Whether you have a fleet of trucks, your own trusty Probox, or a zippy Boda Boda, our renewed Kenya-UK Strategic Partnership is delivering for businesses of all shapes and sizes – we’re going far, together.

Available on Android and iOS, the app brings benefits to all users. Small-scale traders will be empowered to self-declare cargo through simplified declarations, increasing accuracy, transparency and compliance. Passengers will be able to declare customs and accompanied baggage before arrival for faster clearance. Truck drivers and transporter businesses will experience smooth truck rotation and toll-free movement, being able to easily manage declarations for empty trucks and toll collections.

Most importantly of all, this solution provides a basis for the simplification and growth of trade across Kenya and East Africa, with fast-track declarations for goods valued at $2,000 or less. The solution will also support the delivery of the AfCFTA, increasing the efficiency of trade between Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. The app can be downloaded on smartphones and used at all border-crossing points.

The launch bolsters a bumper period for economic relations between Kenya and the UK. A historic milestone was recently reached when data revealed that Kenya-UK trade broke the GBP 2 billion mark for the first time ever. It’s another example of the Kenya-UK Strategic Partnership – which was renewed by UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July 2025 in London - delivering real outcomes for the people of Kenya and the UK.
